target_customer: Small and mid-size US government contractors, later larger GovCon firms, that respond to federal RFPs
problem: Government contractors spend weeks building compliant proposals from past responses and RFP documents.
product_category: AI proposal and capture software for government contracting

founders.name: Akash Mandavilli
prior_employers: Meta (product manager, VR co-presence and WhatsApp ads)
IBM (federal sales operations and predictive analytics)
education: Johns Hopkins University, Economics and Computer Science
founders.background_notes: YC page says the two founders met at Johns Hopkins and built a first startup together; details not found.

founders.name: Gabe Villasana
prior_employers: Johns Hopkins Wilmer Eye Institute (ML research lead)

technical_complexity.rationale: Retrieval and drafting over long RFP documents with Office integrations was standard LLM engineering in early 2023, with harder parts in compliance matrices and later FedRAMP and CMMC security work.

defensibility.rationale: Prompting over customer proposal libraries was easy to copy; stickiness comes from stored past performance data and Office workflow integration, and from later FedRAMP authorization per the company.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent acquisition found by the 2026 searches. Several GovCon AI rivals (pWin.ai, GovDash, Rohirrim, Cleatus) appear in 2025 and 2026 comparisons, which are later entrants not dated to founding.

market_need_then: Federal contractors write large volumes of proposals under tight deadlines; the YC page frames RFP reading and first drafts as the pain. No dated 2023 spend figures were found.

identity.mascot_or_character: Eagle motif implied by the name; not confirmed by a source

brand_strength.rationale: Name signals government and a bald-eagle patriotic cue to the target buyer, but no press about the brand itself was found.

outcome_analysis: GovEagle is still operating as of 2026 with a small 2025 raise of 2.5 million dollars and a FedRAMP Moderate authorization announced in August 2026. The founders' federal sales exposure and the arrival of capable LLMs gave a clear wedge, but the funding found is modest and the field of GovCon AI rivals grew after 2023, so the outcome is still open.
notes: Round stage is not stated by sources so it is recorded as other. Cross-checked by Pulse 2.0 and the company's own blog headline. Sources disagree on founding year (2022 vs 2023) and HQ (New York vs Washington DC). Competition list left empty: no sources dated near the W23 batch were found, only 2025 and 2026 comparisons.
